text: sis, and total lymphoid irradiation.10,13 Inhaled ciclosporin has also been used to treat refractory acute re- jection.1,10 Lung transplant recipients are at high risk of infection as a result of impaired pulmonary defence mechanisms, and post-transplant antibacterial prophylaxis is routine.2 1816 Immunosuppressants Patients at risk for CMV should be given ganciclovir.2,7,12 There is no consensus on standard antifungal prophylaxis after lung transplant, but some centres use oral azole ther- apy or inhaled amphotericin.2 Respiratory viruses pose a substantial risk to the lung allograft,2,4,12 and may contrib- ute to chronic rejection. The main complication encoun- tered in the long term and major cause of late mortality is chronic rejection manifesting as bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome (obliterative bronchiolitis).1,2,7,13 This is charac- terised by progressive airway obstruction and may be present in up to 40% of patients at 2 years, and in 60 to 70% who survive for 5 years.7 Young children and living donor lung transplant recipients may have a lower risk for the development of this syndrome.5 The frequency and se- verity of acute rejection episodes are the main risk factors for the development of bronchiolitis obliterans, but CMV infection, airway ischaemia and HLA mismatching may also play a part.1,4,6,7,12-15 There are no proven effective therapies,4 and the prognosis is poor, with 40% mortality within 3 years of diagnosis.7 Augmentation of immuno- suppression is often tried, but may exacerbate the risk of infection.4 Some centres change the maintenance regimen, converting ciclosporin to tacrolimus, and azathioprine to mycophenolate mofetil, along with a short course of high- dose corticosteroids.10,13 Inhaled ciclosporin has also been used, with reports of a trend towards survival benefit.10 Improvement in pulmonary function has been seen with maintenance azithromycin.10,13,15 Statins may decrease the risk of developing bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome, and promising results have been reported with the use of total lymphoid irradiation.13 Re-transplantation may be neces- sary.4,13 Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorders (PTLD) oc- cur in lung transplant recipients, often in association with a primary Epstein-Barr virus infection.3,4,12 The incidence is high in paediatric patients, ranging from 13 to 20%. Ini- tial treatment involves a reduction in immunosuppression, or chemotherapy with rituximab.3,12 The induction of immune tolerance remains the ultimate goal in lung transplantation.1,11 Combined heart-lung transplants have also been per- formed, see under Heart Transplantation, above. 1.
